name: Lipodissolve / PC-DC injections

lead: Lipodissolve, also called injection lipolysis or PC/DC injections, is the practice of injecting a mixture, usually phosphatidylcholine and sodium deoxycholate, into fat to reduce small deposits such as a double chin, for a leaner jaw and neck.

The detergent-like components are described as disrupting fat cell membranes, causing local breakdown followed by tissue remodeling, and practitioners also report some skin tightening. Published support is mostly retrospective series and practitioner reports, and a review noted that no placebo-controlled studies have established safety or efficacy. A separate FDA-approved deoxycholic acid product (Kybella) exists for submental fullness.

paras: A practitioner injects the mixture into the target area in a series of sessions over weeks, with swelling afterward. It is described as an alternative or add-on to liposuction for small areas.

The FDA stated that lipodissolve products are not approved for fat removal, sent warning letters in 2010, and received reports of scarring, skin deformation and painful lumps. Case reports describe infections, including a nontuberculous mycobacterial infection. Professional societies in plastic surgery and dermatologic surgery have issued warnings.

angle.text: Users have had PC/DC injections to shrink small fat pockets, including under the chin. The mixture breaks down fat cells locally, leaving a leaner jaw and neck. The FDA has warned about these mixtures, and the only approved injectable is a separate deoxycholic acid product.

lead: Lipodissolve, also called injection lipolysis, PC/DC injections or (in some marketing) mesotherapy for fat, is the practice of injecting a drug mixture into the fat layer under the skin with the aim of destroying fat cells in small, localized deposits. Most formulations are based on phosphatidylcholine (PC) and sodium deoxycholate (DC) [1]. For appearance, the target areas are stubborn pockets that diet and exercise leave behind: under the chin, the jowls, the flanks, the abdomen and the upper arms. A smaller submental deposit can blur the jaw-neck angle, so people who want a leaner lower face have looked at it as a non-surgical option.

Practitioner-written papers report reductions in localized fat and some skin retraction, and describe the method as an alternative or adjunct to liposuction [2][3]. A review noted that no placebo-controlled studies have established safety or efficacy, though many retrospective reports describe benefit [1]. In 2010 the US FDA sent warning letters over lipodissolve marketing [1], and professional societies have issued cautions. A related but separate product, deoxycholic acid alone (Kybella), was approved by the FDA in 2015 for moderate to severe fat under the chin [1][4].

paras: In 1966 researchers found that intravenous phosphatidylcholine solutions could clear fat emboli. A product called Lipostabil, containing 5% PC and 2.5% DC, was approved in Germany for conditions such as fat embolism and dyslipidemia. The first report of using it for fat removal described under-eye fat [1].

Use for body contouring spread in the 2000s, and papers in plastic surgery and dermatology journals described techniques and standards of practice [3][5]. In July 2005 a UK malpractice insurer stopped offering cover for its use, and the UK MHRA warned that the drugs were being unlawfully advertised as fat reducers [1]. On April 7, 2010 the FDA sent warning letters to six US medspas and a Brazilian company, stating these products are not approved for fat removal [1].

A 2005 report by practitioners described fat reduction and skin retraction in small deposits, noting outcomes depend on formula, technique and patient selection [2]. A 2012 paper examined safety, effectiveness and patient satisfaction [6], and a 2009 paper described clinical experience with the technique [7]. A 2011 review described the field as having drawn critical scrutiny from media and the FDA, while newer injectables with detergent activity were in development [5]. The Wikipedia summary notes that no placebo-controlled study has shown safety or efficacy [1].

The FDA received reports of permanent scarring, skin deformation and deep painful knots from unapproved lipodissolve products [1]. A 2022 case report described painful purulent nodules caused by Mycobacterium at injection sites [8], and a 2013 case report described hemorrhagic spots on the abdomen after treatment [9]. Professional bodies including the American Society of Plastic Surgeons, the American Society for Aesthetic Plastic Surgery and the American Society of Dermatologic Surgery have issued warnings [1].

A 2013 case report from a toxicology journal described agitation and metabolic acidosis after a lipodissolve injection, and the authors noted that injections were being performed in many countries without legal or scientific evidence of safety and efficacy despite the FDA warning [9]. The Minnesota series described minor and uncommon effects such as pain, tender nodules, pigmentary change and ulceration at injection sites [8]. The FDA's 2010 warning letters also cited claims by clinics that the products could treat male breast enlargement, lipomas and surgical deformities, and the agency stated it knew of no clinical evidence supporting those claims [1].

Lipostabil has been approved in Germany for over 40 years, and the technique is widely used in German-speaking countries, where pharmacies compound the formulations [1]. In the US, deoxycholic acid alone (Kybella) was approved in 2015 for moderate to severe submental fullness, a separate regulatory product from PC/DC mixtures [1].

The deoxycholic acid injection Kybella is marketed by the company Kythera Biopharmaceuticals; Wikipedia records an FDA announcement of 29 April 2015 approving it for fat below the chin, and a generic version in the US from April 2021 [4]. According to the FDA, the PC/DC products used in lipodissolve are not approved for fat removal, and the MHRA has said they cannot lawfully be promoted for that purpose in the UK, though doctors there may still use them [1].

Lipodissolve is delivered as many small injections spread across the treated area, typically over several sessions [1]. Because the products are compounded or imported rather than approved for fat removal, formulations vary between clinics: some use phosphatidylcholine alone, others add deoxycholate, and some practitioners add other ingredients in what is sold as mesotherapy [7][2]. Authors of practice papers have argued that indications, contraindications, expected post-injection swelling and regions to avoid should be standardized [3].

A 2008 review of liposuction technology described chemical lipolysis, under the names mesotherapy or lipodissolve, as a possible alternative to surgery for localized fat while noting that skepticism remains [10]. A French review published in 2006 reported that after a year of use the author considered the method unable to replace liposuction but possibly helpful where liposuction is a poor choice, attributing part of the effect to the inflammatory reaction that follows fat-cell breakdown [11].

Deoxycholate is a bile salt with detergent properties, and phosphatidylcholine is a phospholipid found in cell membranes. Proponents say the mixture disrupts the membranes of fat cells so they break down locally, after which the body clears the contents [1][5]. The 2011 state-of-the-art review described several newer injectables with detergent and lipolytic activity as being in development, after the earlier enthusiasm for mesotherapy and PC/DC was followed by scrutiny from media and the FDA [5].

Fat-dissolving injections are mentioned in appearance communities mainly in connection with the submental area and lower-face fat. As early as 2006, a T Nation forum thread on stubborn love-handle fat described injecting components into fat tissue (under the Lipodissolve name) as one of several spot-reduction approaches, set alongside topical creams and machine-based treatments [12]. In the aesthetics literature, the same technique has also been described for lipomas in a single case with no recurrence at nine months, with the author stating that the approach needs evaluation in larger trials [13].

Published human work consists mainly of practitioner series, reviews and case reports [2][3][5][6][7]. The largest published series came from two collaborating physicians in Minnesota who used a simple phosphatidylcholine-in-deoxycholate solution developed around 2004. Their report covers 1,616 patients and 15,122 treatments, with satisfactory, smooth results in 74.5 to 86.5 percent of patients across the two practices, and the authors report no serious complications [6]. This was an uncontrolled practice series rather than a randomized trial.

Two small trials are registered on ClinicalTrials.gov: an injection lipolysis study for abdominal fat (n=20, started 2008, completed) [14] and a PC/DC study for localized fat removal (n=18, started 2009, terminated) [15]. No results are given in the registration records. A German physicians' network has also collected safety data on tens of thousands of patient results, reported in its 2015 Lipolysis Report [1]. Separately, the registered trials behind the approved deoxycholic acid product are a distinct body of work from PC/DC mixtures [1].
